quote: Maybe it wasn’t that my productivity was unusually chaotic; maybe I was just unusually stupid with respect to predicting it.
content: The reframing has a literature behind it, and the literature is on the essay’s side. Hour-to-hour capacity for cognitive work is patterned by circadian phase and chronotype (Adan et al. (2012)), by ultradian rhythms of roughly ninety minutes, by time since waking and by sleep debt, and these regularities are large enough that individuals who log their own output can find them; the “can’t predict when I’ll be able to work” experience is, in the studies of procrastination and self-regulation, associated with not attending to them (Steel’s meta-analysis, Steel (2007), on the role of task aversiveness and delay). So the essay’s revelation, that the chaos was in the model rather than the process, is plausible for this case and is the kind of thing that self-tracking tests. The annotation is here to note that the essay could have said this, and to mark the difference between the two claims it makes: the specific one, which is supported, and the general one, addressed next.

quote: That’s what inverted stupidity looks like—chaos. Something hard to handle, hard to grasp, hard to guess, something you can’t do anything with. It’s not just an idiom for high abstract things like Artificial Intelligence. It can apply in ordinary life too.
content: The generalization cuts against a technical fact. “Chaos” is not only the name of the feeling that one cannot predict; it is the name of a property of dynamical systems, sensitive dependence on initial conditions, under which prediction beyond a horizon is impossible for any observer with finite measurement precision, however clever (Lorenz (1963)). Whether a given unpredictability is of the first kind (a defect in the observer) or the second (a property of the process relative to any bounded observer) is an empirical question, and the Mind Projection frame the essay invokes has no way to ask it: it assumes that whatever looks like chaos is inverted stupidity, because uncertainty is “in the map.” That is the same move as “uncertainty about initial conditions is really indexical uncertainty” in Is Reality Ugly?, and it has the same cost. Some things are unpredictable to you because you are not paying attention, and some are unpredictable to everyone because the process amplifies noise; the essay’s slogan says the first is always the answer, and the essay’s own anecdote, in which the hours-scale willpower cycle resists “reams and reams of advice” from people who presumably were paying attention, is at least as consistent with the second.
